lesson.title: Essen II: das Obst, die Kartoffel, die Tomate, die Gurke, die Zwiebel
lesson.subtitle: fruit and vegetables — four names that traveled, and one Latin shelf-label

hook.title: Every Name Here Carries a Passport
hook.content: das Obst is the shelf, and everything on it came by a different road. die Kartoffel — the potato — wears an Italian mushroom's name: German borrowed Italian tartufolo, 'truffle', in the 17th century — first as Tartuffel — because the new tuber looked like a truffle growing underground. (English potato is a Caribbean word, Taíno batata through Spanish — the two languages named the same vegetable from two different continents.) die Tomate walked one road in both languages: Nahuatl tomatl, through Spanish tomate, into German and English almost unchanged. die Gurke came overland — German took it from Polish ogórek. die Zwiebel is the old Latin onion, cepa, in its diminutive dress — cepula, 'little onion' — and English kept the same root in the smallest onion of all: the chive. And das Obst itself is Latin obsonium, a word for bought provisions; English took Latin fructus instead and got 'fruit'. Five foods, five roads, one shared table.

footnotes.title: The Earth-Apple
footnotes.content: Before Kartoffel won, German also called the potato das Erdapfel — the earth-apple — the same instinct French had with pomme de terre. The south never gave it up: in Austria and Bavaria the potatoes are still die Erdäpfel, and the compound reads itself — Erd- + Apfel, both words you own.

pattern.title: The Produce Shelf in Sentences
pattern.content: Three frames and a count. 1. The harvest calendar: Im April und im Mai essen wir Tomaten, im September essen wir Gurken, im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln — the month rides behind im and the plural food noun stands bare. 2. The count frame: Eine Million Menschen essen Tomaten — die Million stays singular with bare Menschen after it, exactly as lesson 5122 built it. 3. The category: Obst ist sehr gesund — das Obst is the category (singular, no plural in the shop sense), while die Tomate and die Gurke are the countable pieces. 4. Essen in slot 2, food bare: Ich esse Kartoffeln mit Gemüse.
pattern.linguist_note: Neither language borrowed its potato word from the potato's Andean homeland: English carried a Taíno word through Spanish, German an Italian mushroom name. But the tomato both languages took straight from Nahuatl through Spanish — the rare food that crossed the ocean once and kept its name the whole way.

exercises.prompt: Fruit and vegetables, five roads — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: In April and in May we eat tomatoes
matching_pairs.german: Im April und im Mai essen wir Tomaten

exercises.target_answer: Im April und im Mai essen wir Tomaten, Im September essen wir Gurken, Im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln, Eine Million Menschen essen Tomaten, Obst ist sehr gesund, Ich esse keine Zwiebel, Die Suppe ist heiß
exercises.meaning: tomatoes in spring, cucumbers in September, potatoes in October, a million eaters, healthy fruit, no onions
exercises.explanation: Months ride behind im; die Million stays singular with bare Menschen after it; and das Obst is the category while die Tomate and die Gurke are the countable pieces. Ich esse keine Zwiebel is the picky-eater frame — kein before the bare singular.

exercises.prompt: Which of these four wears a Polish name?
exercises.explanation: Gurke is German's borrowing of Polish ogórek. Kartoffel took the Italian road (tartufolo, 'truffle', in the 1600s), Tomate the Spanish road from Nahuatl, Obst the Latin door — and English gourd is a separate word entirely, from Latin cucurbita, with no family tie to any of them.

exercises.prompt: German 'die Tomate' comes from Nahuatl 'tomatl', which crossed the Atlantic in the 16th century. What is its English twin?
exercises.meaning: die Tomate ↔ tomato: the same Nahuatl word, tomatl
exercises.explanation: Spanish carried Nahuatl tomatl into both languages nearly unchanged — Tomate and tomato are the same word with the last vowel traded. English potato, by contrast, is Taíno batata: a different continent in the same vegetable patch.
Plural Kartoffeln after no article — food stays bare in German. mit introduces what rides along, and the verb keeps slot 2 while the food nouns fill the back of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the harvest sentence: 'In October we eat potatoes and onions'
exercises.target_answer: Im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln und Zwiebeln
exercises.meaning: In October we eat potatoes and onions
exercises.explanation: Time phrase first, verb second, subject third — the order you drilled with the months. Swap Oktober for September and the harvest moves with it: Im September essen wir Gurken.

summary.outcome: Name fruit and vegetables with their genders, put a bare plural on the table, and hang a month behind im.

use_example.german: Im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln — im April und im Mai essen wir Tomaten.
use_example.english: In October we eat potatoes — in April and in May we eat tomatoes.

summary.takeaway: Kartoffel is the truffle's name, Tomate is Nahuatl tomatl, Gurke is Polish ogórek, Zwiebel is Latin cepula (English chive), Obst is Latin obsonium — and Million stays singular before bare Menschen.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the sweet shelf — der Zucker, der Honig, die Schokolade, der Keks, die Torte, and the plural 'cakes' German borrowed whole.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Essen II: das Obst, die Kartoffel, die Tomate, die Gurke, die Zwiebel (In October we eat potatoes and onions):
twist.target_answer: Im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln und Zwiebeln
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Im Oktober essen wir Kartoffeln und Zwiebeln" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Essen II: das Obst, die Kartoffel, die Tomate, die Gurke, die Zwiebel without relying on short-term echo.

obst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *obaet; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

kartoffel.etymology_derivation: From Tartuffel, from Italian tartufolo 'truffle', Latin terrae tūber 'earth tuber'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

tomate.context_phrase: Die Tomate ist rot und reif.
tomate.context_translation: The tomato is red and ripe.
tomate.etymology_derivation: From Spanish/French tomate, Classical Nahuatl tomatl — the same New World loan as English tomato. [wiktionary]

gurke.context_phrase: Die Gurke ist frisch und grün.
gurke.context_translation: The cucumber is fresh and green.
gurke.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, Greek angoúrion — cognate with English gherkin. [wiktionary]

zwiebel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed early from Late Latin cēpulla; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

million.context_phrase: Die Stadt hat eine Million Menschen.
million.context_translation: The city has one million people.
million.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Italian millione — the same Italian loan as English million. [wiktionary]

april.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Aprīlis. [wiktionary]

mai.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin (mensis) Maius via Middle High German meie. [wiktionary]

september.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin September, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

oktober.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Octōber, from octō 'eight' — the eighth month of the old Roman calendar. [wiktionary]

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

suppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Middle Low German suppe under French influence — both trace to Proto-Germanic *supô 'broth'. [wiktionary]

gesund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *sundaz — the same root as English sound, as in safe and sound. [wiktionary]

mensch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *manniskaz 'human', built on Mann — English mannish is the cognate form. [wiktionary]

hängen.context_phrase: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
hängen.context_translation: The picture hangs on the wall.
hängen.etymology_derivation: A merger of three old hang-verbs, back to Proto-Germanic *hanhaną and *hangijaną; the page documents cognate English hang — strong like hang-hung (hing, gehangen). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
